title: Mood Tag
summary: A told tale carries a mood whether the teller plans it or not. This kit listens for the difference between a stated mood ('this is scary!') and a felt mood (the room's quiet at the right moment).

questions.prompt: What mood did you tag your tale? Funny, scary, tender, or wild? Now play back the first 20 seconds. Could a listener tell the mood without you naming it?
Which line makes the mood FELT, not just stated?
options: It was really sad when grandma left.
The kitchen kept being the same kitchen, and grandma's spot at the table kept being empty.
I felt very tender about my grandma.
questions.rationale: Tender moods land in the specific image, not the word 'tender'. The empty spot does the work.

questions.prompt: Tell the same 30-second story with a different mood. Same events, different room temperature. What changed in your voice?
Take a funny moment from your tale and write a 'wild' version of the same moment. Keep the events; change the energy.

castCameos.line: Saying the mood-image twice — once at the open, once at the close — locks the mood in. Try it.
When the mood is felt and not stated, my body still tips forward — sometimes harder.
A mood-flip is its own kind of turn. Watch for it.
Close slows. A tender mood needs the last line to land softly, not punch.
